coachingPoints: The back foot is your pivot foot — it must stay planted until you decide your move.
Keep the steps short; long strides carry you into the defender.
Stay low through the stop — standing up kills your balance.
Ball protected on the outside hip as you stride in.
Use the stride stop to create separation, not just to stop — step away from the defender.
commonMistakes: Sliding the pivot foot — that's a travel; the back foot is glued down.
Taking three steps instead of two — count it out loud until it's automatic.
Landing upright with straight knees — no balance, no explosion.
Striding directly into the defender's chest instead of stepping past or away.
description: The one-two step stop: back foot plants, front foot lands — control, separation, and a ready pivot.
gameSituations: Pull-up jumpers off the dribble — the stride stop is the classic pull-up footwork.
Driving to a spot against a retreating defender — stop and rise before they recover.
Post catches on the move — land in a stride and face up.

howTo.detail: As you approach your spot, pick up the ball with two hands. You have two steps to stop — plan them before you gather.
howTo.title: Gather with two steps in mind

howTo.detail: Plant your first step (usually the back foot) firmly, slightly outside your shoulder line. This foot becomes your pivot foot.
howTo.title: Step one: plant the back foot

howTo.detail: Bring your second foot forward and plant it, arriving in a staggered stance — knees bent, weight balanced between both feet, ball in triple threat.
howTo.title: Step two: stride and land

howTo.detail: From this stance you can shoot, pivot on the back foot, or drive. The staggered base gives you forward explosion that a jump stop doesn't.
howTo.title: Read and explode

title: Stride Stop
whatIsIt: The stride stop is a two-step stop: plant the back foot, then stride the front foot forward, landing in a staggered stance. It's the 'one-two' rhythm behind pull-up jumpers and controlled drives.

Unlike the jump stop, the stride stop keeps your momentum flowing forward. That's why shooters love it — you stop and rise into the shot in one continuous motion instead of landing flat and starting over.
whyItMatters: Almost every pull-up jumper in basketball is finished with a stride stop. It lets you stop on balance while keeping your shooting rhythm, and it leaves you with a legal pivot foot. Players who master both stops — jump and stride — can finish any drive situation.
